figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Speedup over AR with one request. SpecPilot more than doubles stock’s speedup in each setting.
figures.headline: SpecPilot more than doubles stock's single-request speedup over AR in every setting shown.
citing_sentences: Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock’s 4.46$\times$ to 10.87$\times$ with one request (Figure 1), and from 1.94$\times$ to 3.93$\times$ with batching.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: (a) Single-request step time split into target weights and the rest, at peak bandwidth and as measured after the first optimization round. Reading the weights dominates the step. (b) Stock speedup over AR falls as the batch size grows, for Qwen3.8-27B in FP8 and Qwen3.5-4B in BF16. (c) Task accuracy change against stock, with 95% CIs, for a lossless system and a faulty one with an injected logit bias. All four intervals include zero, so accuracy cannot flag the faulty systems.
figures.headline: Accuracy changes cannot separate faulty from lossless systems, since all four confidence intervals include zero.
citing_sentences: With one request, reading the target weights dominates the per-step latency (Figure 2a), so verifying additional tokens adds little extra latency.
With batching, each request adds its own attention, recurrent-state and prefill work, so weight reads no longer dominate the step, and stock’s speedup over AR decoding roughly halves (Figure 2b).
Second, an agent rewarded for speed is prone to reward hacking [19, 20], such as adopting a faster numerical shortcut that changes outputs without a measurable drop in task accuracy (Figure 2c).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: One round of the SpecPilot loop. 0 The cost model measures the gap between the current system and its ceiling. 1 Directions run in parallel, one per GPU. 2 Validated pieces stack into one system. 3 A kernel sub-agent tunes the kernels furthest from their byte floors. 4 Token forcing checks the sealed final against stock at every teacher-forced token. Each round distills its mechanisms into memory entries, which carry to later rounds and new deployments.
figures.headline: One SpecPilot round measures the gap to the ceiling, runs parallel directions, stacks validated pieces and checks the sealed final.
citing_sentences: We present SpecPilot (Figure 3), an autonomous agentic loop that searches for speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment.
SpecPilot separates the agents that modify the system from the controller that measures it (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Token forcing on lossless and faulty systems in sealed finals. Bars give the mismatch rate with 95% CIs, and dashed lines the rate-rule limit. Above the bars are the verdict and the count of large-margin events. Faulty systems add a logit bias of 2 to every 7th vocabulary id after 2048 tokens.
figures.headline: Token forcing results compare lossless systems with faulty ones that receive an injected logit bias after 2048 tokens.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 tests lossless and faulty systems.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: W12. (a) Each BF16 weight becomes three 4-bit planes: A holds the sign and the top three mantissa bits, E a 4-bit exponent offset within a 16-binade window per output channel, and B the low mantissa bits. A and E form the 8-bit view that the Q pass of two-level verification reads. The remaining weights, a fraction of $7.3\times 10^{-5}$ on Qwen3.8-27B, go to an exact escape list. (b) The GEMM decodes W12 records in registers and feeds them to wgmma as the register operand.
figures.headline: W12 splits each BF16 weight into three 4-bit planes, with the few remaining weights kept in an exact escape list.
citing_sentences: In round two, step cost led (§6.1), so the master opened a direction cutting weight bytes (W12, Figure 5).
Each weight with in-window exponent $e$ is stored as its sign bit, a 4-bit exponent offset $e-(E_{n}-15)$, and its seven mantissa bits, for a total of 12 bits (Figure 5a).
A stream-K kernel (Figure 5b) splits the reduction loop over thread blocks in a fixed order, so the GEMM is deterministic.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Best-first tree on a hybrid target. On the same lattice, stock verifies only the greedy chain, which stops at its first miss. The best-first tree keeps the $N$ nodes with the highest path score $\sum\log p(\mathrm{child}\mid\mathrm{parent})$, so another candidate can continue. On hybrid targets, each root path recomputes its GDN state. The right panel compares the path and WY verify kernels over 48 GDN layers on H100.
figures.headline: A best-first tree keeps candidates that a greedy chain drops, and a faster verify kernel is compared against the path kernel.
citing_sentences: Round one built best-first trees (Figure 6) on the DFlash2 lattice, scoring each edge by $\log\mathrm{softmax}$ of selector scores given its parent, not by DDTree’s marginal scores [10].

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Two-level verification. A low-precision Q pass checks the draft tree and returns chain C, the path that matches the Q pass’s argmax plus a bonus token, without updating the target’s state. The drafter drafts again from the end of C, and one exact pass over the W12 weights verifies C and the new subtree. Times are from one final H100 cycle, and tokens per exact pass from TLV’s round. The right panel shows the 8-bit view nested in each W12 record, which the Q pass reads.
figures.headline: Two-level verification uses a low-precision pass to build a chain, then one exact pass verifies the combined tree.
citing_sentences: Each TLV cycle has two passes (Figure 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Single-request Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 on H100 over three rounds. Filled points mark steps of the algorithms in §4.1–4.3.
figures.headline: Single-request speedup across three rounds is shown with algorithm steps from the discovered mechanisms marked as filled points.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: W12 beyond speculative decoding, on H100. (a) AR decoding speedup over BF16 weights in SGLang with one request. (b) Weight memory in BF16 and W12. (c) W12 GEMM speedup over cuBLAS on Qwen3.8-27B projections at 1 and 32 rows, with cold L2.
figures.headline: W12 alone raises autoregressive decoding speed and cuts weight memory, shown alongside matrix-multiply speedups per row count.

figures.caption: Tokens per step $\tau$ in exact replay of single-request DFlash2 on Qwen3.8-27B, against the number of verified nodes $N$. Best-first trees run on lattices drafted with 8 and 16 positions. The gray line is stock’s 8-position chain, and the oracle on the 16-position lattice reaches 8.2 tokens per step.
figures.headline: Best-first trees on 8- and 16-position lattices are compared with stock's chain, and the 16-position oracle reaches 8.2 tokens per step.

figures.caption: Sealed gains over stock on unseen requests. (a) Single request, per benchmark. (b) Batching on H100, per batch size.

figures.caption: Batching on H100, per batch size, measured on the interleaved bench. (a) Speedup over AR of stock and SpecPilot. (b) Tokens per step $\tau$ of stock and SpecPilot.

abstract:
Abstract

Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock’s 4.46$\times$ to 10.87$\times$ with one request, and from 1.94$\times$ to 3.93$\times$ with batching.

sections.body: Parallel drafters such as DFlash2, DFlash and DSpark draft a block of 8 or 16 tokens per forward pass, but their released systems (stock) leave much of this speedup unrealized. With one request, reading target weights dominates each step, and stock verifies only one drafted chain. With batching, stock's speedup over AR roughly halves. Speculative decoding behaves differently across deployments, so the paper proposes SpecPilot, an agentic loop that uses a cost model, parallel agents, token forcing against stock, and structured memory. Reported results are 4.46× to 10.87× with one request and 1.94× to 3.93× with batching, without training or quality loss.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Stock parallel-drafter systems leave speedup unrealized, which motivates SpecPilot's per-deployment search.

sections.body: Background defines speculative decoding: a drafter proposes tokens and the target verifies them in one pass, accepting a greedy prefix plus a bonus token. A system is lossless only if every accepted token lies on a path verified by the exact target weights and matches its argmax. Stock already differs from AR at near-ties, where the two tokens' log-probabilities differ by at most 0.232 nats. Parallel drafters such as DSpark add a Markov head on the previous token, and draft trees verify several candidates per step. Hybrid targets such as Qwen3.8-27B use Gated DeltaNet layers, whose recurrent state must be tracked for each tree node. Requiring identical outputs rejects lossless systems and accuracy misses faulty ones, so token forcing checks each token statistically against stock.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Lossless speculative decoding accepts only tokens matching the exact target's argmax, so output tests cannot easily verify it.

sections.body: SpecPilot runs in rounds: a cost model measures the gap between the current system and its ceiling, parallel agents build and time changes, and a sealed final on unseen requests ends each round. The cost model expresses speedup over AR as tokens accepted per step divided by step time relative to AR. On stock DFlash2 with one request, exact replay accepts 4.25 tokens per step, while an oracle reaches 6.42 at 8 positions and 8.20 at 16. After the first round, reading target weights took 80% of the measured 23.61 ms step. A change is promoted only if its gain's 95% lower bound exceeds 1% plus twice the stock-versus-stock noise, and token forcing gates every patch.
sections.heading: SpecPilot
sections.headline: A cost model finds the largest gap to a ceiling, and a controller accepts changes only on confirmed gains.

sections.body: Each mechanism in this section is lossless. W12 keeps each weight's exponent within a 16-binade window per output channel, storing 12 bits per weight, with 12.01–12.02 bits on eight dense models. It reduces Qwen3.8-27B's converted layers from 44.67 to 33.58 GB. The certified LM head cut latency from 878 to 482 µs on H100, but on RTX PRO 6000 it was slower (2598 vs. 1750 µs), so W12 converts that head there. Best-first trees recompute recurrent state along each root path, and a faster verify kernel handles hybrid targets. Two-level verification uses the 8-bit view inside W12 as a low-precision check, which matches the exact pass's top-1 token at 98.7% of positions. Batching uses a shared node budget of 192 nodes on FP8 targets.
sections.heading: Discovered Lossless Algorithms
sections.headline: SpecPilot discovered a lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification, two-level verification and batching mechanisms.

sections.body: Evaluation covers Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 and DSpark, Muse-Glimmer-30B, Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-12B, on five benchmarks, using sealed finals on unseen requests. Table 3 gives single-request sealed gains of 2.13× for Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 on H100, 2.38× with DSpark on H100, and 2.44× with DFlash2 on RTX PRO 6000. Batching gains on H100 range from 1.85× to 3.11×. For Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 on H100, single-request decoding rises from 183.9 tokens per second for stock to 416.1 with SpecPilot. Interleaved runs fall within −2% to +6% of the sealed gains. Every final system passed token forcing.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Sealed finals on unseen requests give single-request gains of 2.13× to 2.44× and batching gains of 1.85× to 3.11×.
